nameStory: The striped skunk gets its name from the unmistakable white stripes that run down its black back, making it one of the most recognizable animals in North America. The scientific name 'Mephitis' comes from Latin meaning 'bad odor' or 'noxious vapor' — a not-so-subtle reference to their famous defensive spray! It's nature's way of advertising: 'Look at my bold stripes and stay away!'
description: The striped skunk is a cat-sized mammal famous for its distinctive black fur with white stripes and its ability to spray a pungent musk when threatened. About the size of a house cat but stockier and lower to the ground, skunks have small heads, short legs, and fluffy tails they can raise like a warning flag. These adaptable omnivores eat everything from insects and small mammals to fruits and garbage, making them successful neighbors to humans throughout New England. Despite their fearsome reputation, they're generally gentle creatures that prefer to mind their own business.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Glossy black fur with two prominent white stripes running from head to tail, plus a white patch on the forehead. The fur feels coarse and dense, with longer guard hairs over softer undercoat that helps them stay warm in winter.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: House cat-sized but built low and sturdy, about 2-3 feet long with short, stubby legs. The body appears chunky and rounded, with a small pointed head that seems almost too small for the body.

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Large, fluffy black tail with white on the tip and sides that they hold high like a bottle brush when threatened. The tail is nearly as long as their body and serves as their warning signal.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Five-toed prints about 2 inches long showing long claws, especially on front feet used for digging. Tracks often show a pigeon-toed gait with hind feet stepping beside rather than into front prints.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Waddles with an unhurried, confident gait and rarely runs. When threatened, they stamp their front feet, raise their tail, and may do a handstand before spraying their infamous musk.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small cone-shaped holes in lawns from digging for grubs, and cylindrical scat containing insect parts, seeds, and fur. You might also detect their musky odor lingering in areas they frequent.

habitat: Striped skunks thrive in mixed habitats throughout New England, from suburban neighborhoods and farmland to woodland edges and brushy areas. They prefer areas that offer both open space for foraging and cover for denning, such as barns, sheds, rock piles, or burrows under porches. You'll often find them near water sources and in areas rich with insects, their favorite food.

seasonality.spring: Most active season as they emerge from winter dens and begin breeding. Look for fresh digging in lawns as they hunt for grubs and emerging insects, plus increased road sightings as males search for mates.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with families of mothers and kits foraging together at dusk and dawn. Young skunks are learning to spray, so you might notice more skunk odor in the air during evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily to build fat reserves for winter, often raiding garbage cans and pet food. Their fur becomes thicker and more lustrous as they prepare for cold weather.
seasonality.winter: Least active season as they enter a state of dormancy (not true hibernation) in dens, emerging on warmer days. Look for tracks in snow leading to and from den sites under buildings or in brush piles.

funFact: A skunk can accurately spray its musk up to 15 feet away, and the smell can be detected by humans from over a mile downwind — but they only carry enough 'ammunition' for about 5-6 sprays before needing several days to reload!
confusionNotes: Sometimes confused with black cats at night, but skunks have white markings, move with a distinctive waddle, and hold their tails high. Remember: if you see white stripes and a bottle-brush tail, give it plenty of space!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their reputation, skunks are actually beneficial neighbors that eat tons of garden pests like grubs, beetles, and rodents. They've been featured in countless cartoons and children's books, usually as the character everyone avoids, but in reality they're quite docile and only spray as a last resort when they feel truly threatened.
compareHints: The striped skunk is the only skunk species found in New England, making it unique among our local carnivores. While they're related to weasels and badgers, skunks are much stockier and slower-moving, with their bold warning coloration being the opposite of most weasel family members who rely on stealth and speed rather than chemical defense.
